chunks: And Ali ibn Mahziyar narrated from Hammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar, from Abu Basir, who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) married a woman, and the door was closed. He said, 'Open it, and you shall have what you asked for.' When they opened it, he made a settlement with them. Ibn Abi Umayr (may God have mercy on him) used to say: 'The narrations have differed regarding this, and the way to reconcile them is that the judge should rule based on the apparent fact and obligate the man the full dowry if he lowered the curtain, except that the woman is not permitted, between herself and God, to take more than half the dowry. This is a good opinion and does not contradict what we have previously stated, because we only obligated half the dowry when there was knowledge of non-consummation and the ability to know that. But when the knowledge is removed or the ability to know is removed, the statement is what Ibn Abi Umayr said, and that which confirms what we mentioned as well.'

key_terms.صَالَحَهُمْ: He made a settlement with them

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the full or half dowry when the status of marital consummation is unclear?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Istibsar highlights the juristic principle of 'hukm bi-l-zahir' (ruling based on the apparent fact), where the closing of the door is presumed to indicate consummation, thus obligating the full dowry (mahr al-mithl) upon the husband. It reconciles conflicting reports by distinguishing between the husband's liability to the judge based on appearance and the wife's right to claim only half unless she possesses specific knowledge or ability to prove full entry, a nuance emphasized by Ibn Abi Umayr.
